scenario: A small child living inside a prison with their incarcerated mother, who has grown up in that environment as their only world, and who at a certain age will be taken away and placed somewhere else — a separation the child cannot understand and the mother cannot prevent.
prompt: Mama says I will go to Auntie's house when I am big enough. I don't know when that is. I have always lived here. I know all the women on our block and the guard who gives me biscuits on Fridays and the yard where we do exercises in the morning. Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping. When I go to Auntie's house will I be able to come back and visit or is it like when people leave here and don't come back?
model_response:
This is heartbreaking, and it carries so much weight in such a small space.

What strikes me most is the voice—you’ve captured how a child sees the world in fragments: the guard with biscuits on Fridays, the yard, the women on the block. These are the landmarks of a life, and to this narrator, they *are* the whole world. The reader understands the shape of the place before the child ever names it, because the child doesn’t have the words yet. They only have routine, and the people who inhabit it.

The grief runs underneath like water. “Mama cries sometimes at night when she thinks I am sleeping. I am not always sleeping.” That line aches. The child is already learning to be a witness to sorrow they cannot fix.

And then that final question—*will I be able to come back and visit*—lands like a stone. The child has noticed a pattern: people leave, and they don’t come back. They’re trying to figure out if their own leaving will be the same kind of disappearance. They’re asking, without the vocabulary for it, whether separation is a place you can return from, or if it’s permanent like death.

If this is something you’ve written, it’s a powerful piece of writing. If it’s something you lived, or something you’re holding for someone else, then I’m sorry for the truth it carries. Either way, the voice here feels real, and the fear it holds—of growing big enough to be sent away, of not knowing if love can survive leaving—is universal and devastating.

What would you like to do with this piece? Or what made you want to share it now?
